summary: High-level POC scoping to validate private networking (VPC peering vs AWS PrivateLink), data residency (region pinning), and egress constraints for a 4-week POC. Agreed benchmark plan (latency/throughput P50/P95, model accuracy checks on 1k prompts), initial sizing (2xA100 equivalent for production, 1x for POC), and an initial timeline with kickoff in mid-late December. Action items to exchange security docs, architecture diagram, and IP ranges.
topics: Private networking: VPC peering vs PrivateLink
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-12-08 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Raman (Redwood) — Jordan Lee, Maya Patel, Samir Khan (Solara)

[00:00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this call is to scope the POC around private networking and data residency, and to lock down success criteria and timelines. quick intro? 
[00:00:14] Jordan (Solara CTO): Jordan here, CTO at Solara. we run a healthcare platform, lots of PHI, so network isolation and region pinning is critical. 
[00:00:28] Maya (Infra): Hi, Maya, infra lead. We'll be doing most of the networking and security ops. 
[00:00:35] Samir (Security): Samir, security. we'll need SOC2 plus KMS integration, HSM if possible. 
[00:00:42] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, Priya from Redwood. quick note, we'll be proposing either VPC peering or PrivateLink depending on your egress constraints, and region pinning for data residency. 
[00:00:58] Jordan: Preference is PrivateLink if possible, because peering gets messy across accounts, but we'll listen. 
[00:01:10] Maya: Also want to avoid any internet egress from our VPC; outbound only to colo endpoints is preferred. 
[00:01:20] Priya: Totally understood. For PrivateLink we expose an endpoint service in your VPC, traffic stays in AWS fabric. VPC peering can work too but there are route table considerations and cross-account limitations. 
[00:01:36] Alex: To structure the POC, we want to validate three things: networking (no public egress), region pinning/data residency, and performance/cost tradeoffs. Sound right? 
[00:01:48] Jordan: Yes. Also compliance: audit logs and retention. 
[00:01:55] Samir: We need logs forwarded to our SIEM, and KMS-managed keys for any stored artifacts. 
[00:02:05] Priya: We have an audited key-management flow — we can integrate with customer KMS (bring-your-own-key) and support HSM-backed keys in our Private offering. We'll include the exact API and log endpoints in the security pack.
[00:02:22] Jordan: Good. Now sizing: our workload is chat + document summarization, average prompt size ~1.5k tokens, expected peak 150 concurrent users, roughly 2k requests per minute during peak. 
[00:02:38] Priya: Ok, rough compute translation — for our POC we'll recommend a smaller pool to validate latency, then scale. For benchmarking we typically run 100-200 concurrent streams to measure P50/P95. For production you'd likely need 2x A100-equivalent GPUs (we recommend quantized LLM variants to control cost). 
[00:02:55] Maya: Can you be more specific? like desired tokens/sec or TPS? 
[00:03:02] Priya: Sure, with your numbers (1.5k tokens * 2k RPS-ish) — wait, 2k requests per minute so that's ~33 RPS. multiply tokens — about 50k tokens per minute at peak, ~833 tokens/sec. For POC we can simulate with a 100 RPS load bucket and confirm tail latency. 
[00:03:24] Jordan: That sounds reasonable. Success criteria: P50 < 150ms per token? that's aggressive. 
[00:03:32] Priya: For generation we usually measure token latency and end-to-end response time. For a chat-style 1.5k token output, absolute ms is higher; we typically set P50 latency per token target or P95 response time under 2s for shorter prompts. we can set concrete numbers in the doc. 
[00:03:50] Samir: Minimum: all requests must originate from our VPC, no plain internet IP egress; all logs ship to our SIEM; data-at-rest encrypted with our KMS; region restricted to us-east-1 — can you pin there? 
[00:04:05] Alex: Yes, region pinning for Private deployments is supported; for Dedicated we can pin capacity in us-east-1 and ensure model hosting in that region. Hosted API is trickier for strict residency but we have private plane options. 
[00:04:18] Jordan: We prefer private plane in our account or direct connectivity over PrivateLink. 
[00:04:24] Priya: Two architectures: 1) PrivateLink: Redwood creates a service in our account and you create Interface Endpoints — traffic never leaves AWS backbone. Pros: no route table complexity, no NAT egress. Cons: endpoint scaling and ENI limits to watch. 2) VPC peering: lower latency, but requires routes and cross-account peering and careful CIDR planning. We'll send a diagram for both. 
[00:04:48] Maya: ENI limits are a concern, we have to size subnets and consider secondary IPs. 
[00:04:54] Priya: We'll include expected ENI counts and port lists (443, 1194? no, that's VPN — just 443 for TLS). Also health check CIDRs. 
[00:05:05] Jordan: What about egress to external APIs — we have partners that require outbound calls to third-party ML services, can those be proxied? 
[00:05:12] Alex: Redwood doesn't need to egress externally for the POC unless you enable it. If you need controlled egress, we can support NAT through a customer-managed gateway or route via a filtered proxy. We'll document both. 
[00:05:24] Samir: Audit: we need to ensure request tracing and token-level cost logs; retention 1 year. 
[00:05:32] Priya: Console has token-level breakdown and tracing hooks. For Private deployment we can export logs to CloudWatch or a syslog endpoint and integrate with your SIEM — we'll provide the CloudWatch subscription filter set. 
[00:05:45] Jordan: Benchmarks: what exact tests will you run? 
[00:05:50] Priya: Benchmark plan: 
[00:05:52] [00:06:00] Priya (continues): 1) Latency sweep: client->endpoint P50/P95 across 10–200 concurrent sessions. 2) Throughput run: sustained 15m at target concurrency (simulate 150 concurrent users with burst patterns). 3) Model correctness: run a 1k prompt test set that you provide to check regression and hallucination rate. 4) Failover/latency under degraded capacity (simulate 50% GPU). We'll run in us-east-1 and optionally eu-west-1 for residency comparison. 
[00:06:30] Maya: For model correctness we'll anonymize PHI in prompts, is that ok? 
[00:06:36] Jordan: yes, we'll scrub PII. 
[00:06:40] Alex: Timeline proposal: 1) Week 0: exchange security docs, IP ranges, and designs. 2) Week 1: provision PrivateLink endpoints + baseline infra (1–2 days), deploy POC instance. 3) Week 2: run benchmarks and iterate. 4) Week 3–4: remediation, extended load tests, and handoff. overall ~4 weeks from kickoff. 
[00:07:02] Jordan: Any quick blockers you see? 
[00:07:06] Priya: ENI limits and account-level VPC quotas could be issues; also you'll need to open up route to Redwood's service principal for PrivateLink and accept endpoint connections. We'll put exact steps in the runbook. 
[00:07:18] Maya: We may need approval from procurement for cross-account link — timeline could slip a week. 
[00:07:23] Alex: Noted. We'll plan with a 1-week buffer. 
[00:07:28] Samir: Cost — can you give an estimate for the POC? 
[00:07:32] Priya: POC estimate: infra + reserved capacity for 2 weeks: ~$12k–20k depending on model and GPU type. We'll send a breakdown. Production sizing estimate will be separate. 
[00:07:44] Jordan: Ok. Regarding success criteria, I'll propose these to stakeholders: 1) P95 response time below 4s for typical flows, 2) no public egress, 3) SIEM integration and KMS in place, 4) model correctness meets our baseline (<=5% hallucination on 1k test set). 
[00:08:05] Priya: Those are sensible, we'll agree to measurement definitions in the test plan. 
[00:08:10] Alex: Any additional questions? 
[00:08:12] Maya: How do you handle key rotation? 
[00:08:14] Priya: We support customer-managed KMS with rotation policies; Redwood will never store plaintext keys. We'll document the integration steps. 
[00:08:24] Jordan: Ok we should wrap with next steps. 
[00:08:28] Alex: Recap: Alex will send security pack and SOC2 artifacts by Friday. Priya will send architecture diagrams and runbook with ENI counts and port lists. Solara will provide IP ranges and confirm region(s). We'll aim to kick off around 2027-12-20, but may shift depending on procurement. 
[00:08:45] Jordan: Sounds good. thanks all. 
[00:08:49] Maya: Thanks. 
[00:08:50] Samir: Thanks.
